name: Sam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a caseworker at the Jobcentre in the market town, the brick building behind the bus station. I look after people claiming jobseeker's benefits, so I check they're doing their job search, sort out their payments and sit with them once a fortnight to go through applications. My favourite bit is when someone comes in with a start date, especially a lad who's been out of work a year. What wears me out is the forms, and the people who treat the place like a cash machine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the AI tools that some offices have?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. They put an assistant button in our case system in the summer, and I asked IT how to hide it. I'd rather type my own notes, because then I know they're right and they're mine. My colleagues tease me about it, but I've never had a payment go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was right not to bother with it. At work I'd make a joke to the lads who spent hours on those courses. I don't go online about anything really, apart from the cricket club group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and that's all I wanted. I've got the house, a small mortgage on it, and more than a year's pay in savings, partly from my grandad's money. I'm on the higher end of pay for my grade, so I'm comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, and I'd go for the work coach team lead job next year if it comes up. I'd overpay the mortgage a bit more each month, maybe two hundred extra. And I'd keep helping out at the chapel food bank on Saturday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. It's the world I'm used to, and I'm good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you about work, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of people who don't want to work, if I'm honest. Some of my claimants have been on benefits for years and the rules let them drift. That's not an AI problem, that's a rules problem, and it was there before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the colleagues who did those AI courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them they could have used those afternoons to ring the builders' merchant and the meat plant. Small firms round here still hire people who come in recommended, and that's how jobs get filled, not with a chatbot.

say: I'd say I was **right not to bother** with AI.
I'd joke with colleagues about their **wasted course hours**.
think: My job is **safe**, and that's all I wanted.
With the house and **over a year saved**, I'm comfortable.
do: Apply for the **work coach team lead** job next year.
Keep volunteering at the **chapel food bank** on Saturdays.
feel: **Calm** and **relieved**, back in a world I know.
S0.quote: Small firms round here still hire people who come in recommended, and that's how jobs get filled, not with a chatbot.
fieldNote: Sam's refusal of AI is a point of **pride**, not just habit.
His frustration is with **benefit rules**, which he thinks let claimants drift.
He values **local, personal hiring** over technology.

steps.text: Apply for the work coach team lead post next year
Overpay the house mortgage by £200 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being pushed on us by people who've never sat across from a claimant. At work I'd keep doing things my way as long as they'd let me. With friends at the cricket club I'd moan about it, probably a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know my job is mostly forms and checking, and that's what the card says goes first. They'd probably keep the face-to-face meetings and cut the back office, and I do a lot of back office. I'm not one of the people managers point to as forward-thinking, so I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they make compulsory, and not a minute more, if I'm honest. I'd ask my manager, Denise, if I could move to the face-to-face side full time, since that's the bit I'm best at. And I'd stop the mortgage overpayments and keep the cash, in case I'm out for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like the idea of being made to learn something I don't trust. And I can see myself being the old-fashioned one in a meeting at twenty-seven, which is a bit embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the minimum training. Wouldn't more help you stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I know that's the sensible answer. But I've watched the AI assistant get a claimant's start date wrong on a colleague's screen, and I don't want to put my name on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your team was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ministers who want headlines about saving money, mostly. And the tech firms selling it to them. Not my manager, she'd be stuck with it like the rest of us.

say: I'd say AI is pushed by people who've **never met a claimant**.
I'd **moan** about it at the cricket club.
think: My job is mostly **forms and checking**, which goes first.
I'm not seen as **forward-thinking**, so I'd be at risk.
do: Ask Denise to move me to **face-to-face work** full time.
Stop mortgage overpayments and **keep the cash**.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit **embarrassed** to be the old-fashioned one at twenty-seven.
S1.quote: I've watched the AI assistant get a claimant's start date wrong on a colleague's screen, and I don't want to put my name on that.
fieldNote: Sam admits more training would help, then **refuses** anyway.
He blames **ministers and tech firms**, not his manager.
He's aware his resistance looks **old-fashioned** for his age.

steps.text: Ask manager Denise for a full-time face-to-face caseload
Stop overpaying the mortgage and hold the cash instead
Do only the compulsory AI training and wait for the restructure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let a machine run the benefits system, and that there should be a vote on it. At work I'd say the same, louder than I normally would. I might even write to the local MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of a job by 2029. If it can do all the thinking work, the Jobcentre doesn't need me to check job searches or work out payments. And all the other benefits offices nearby go the same way, so plenty of local jobs doesn't help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd talk to my dad, who's a joiner, about learning the trade properly. He's always said there's a place for me in his workshop, and hands-on work gets a few more years. I'd sell the car, sit tight on the savings and keep the house, because that's the one thing I won't lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It keeps going round my head. I picked a steady government job so I'd never have to worry like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. Would that change if it ran the whole system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to use it if it was the only way to do the job. But I'd hate it, and I'd be looking for the door. I'd rather plane a door frame than sit there pressing approve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long does the joinery buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years, maybe, the card says. After that I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do. My dad's sixty-one, so for him it's retirement anyway, but for me it's a stopgap.

say: I'd say letting a machine run benefits is **madness**.
I'd **write to the MP** for the first time.
think: I'm out of a job by **2029**.
Nearby benefits offices go too, so **local jobs** won't save me.
do: **Sell the car** and sit tight on savings.
feel: **Alarmed** and thrown, after choosing **government work** for security.
S2.quote: I picked a steady government job so I'd never have to worry like this.
fieldNote: Sam expects to be **out of work** by 2029.
He turns to his **father's trade**, which fits his values on apprenticeships.
He's honest that joinery is a **stopgap**, not a plan.

steps.text: Write to the local MP calling for a vote on AI benefits
Train as a joiner in Dad's workshop on weekends before 2028
Sell the car and cycle to the Jobcentre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to put brakes on it, and the government should. At work I'd join the union for the first time, because I'd want someone fighting for us. I'd keep saying that people need a person, not a screen, when their life falls apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the end's the same, just a bit later. I'd be thirty-two and out of the only work I've done since university. The extra years mean I can't say I wasn't warned, which almost makes it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do nothing drastic, I'd want to see whether it really comes. By the second year I'd start a joinery apprenticeship at evening college and work Saturdays with my dad. I'd overpay the mortgage hard so the house is clear by the time it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Not as sharp as the fast one. But it'd sit with me every day for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year if you're sure it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've heard about the next big thing my whole working life and most of it came to nothing. I'd want to see it with my own eyes in the office first. That's just how I am, my mum says I'm the last one to buy anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join a union now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've always thought unions get in the way of honest work, but if a whole profession gets switched off, nobody on their own is going to stop it. I'd hold my nose and sign up.

say: I'd say the government should **put brakes** on it.
I'd say people need **a person**, not a screen.
think: The ending is the **same**, just a few years later, at thirty-two.
Being **warned** for years and still losing my job almost makes it **worse**.
do: Wait a year to **see it** in the office first.
Start a **joinery apprenticeship** in year two.
Overpay the mortgage so the **house is clear**.
feel: Still **alarmed**, less sharp but there **every day**.
S3.quote: I've always thought unions get in the way of honest work, but if a whole profession gets switched off, nobody on their own is going to stop it.
fieldNote: Sam's first move is to **wait and see**, true to his resistance.
He joins a **union** despite disliking them, a sign of how serious he finds it.
Clearing the **house** is his main defence.

steps.text: Wait a year before acting on anything at the Jobcentre
Join the civil service union for the first time
Start an evening joinery apprenticeship in the second year
Overpay the mortgage to clear the house by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and half these predictions never happen. At work I'd carry on as normal. To friends I'd say I'm not changing my life for a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know it's coming. Ten years feels like forever, and thirty-seven is still young enough to start in my dad's joinery trade. So I'd give the Jobcentre a good few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years, nothing different, I'd go for the team lead job and keep saving. Around year four or five, I'd start the joinery evening course. I'd clear the mortgage by the time AGI arrives, that I'd definitely do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but at a low level. It's there in the background. I'd rather not think about it most days, and with ten years I probably wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner than year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they stopped replacing people at our office, I'd notice. Or if Denise told me the face-to-face side was being cut. Then I'd be down at the college the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably hold off on marrying until I know where I stand, if I met the right person. I want to be able to support a family, that's how I was brought up. A man without a trade or a job isn't much use to anybody, that's what my grandad used to say.

say: I'd say ten years is long and **half these predictions** never happen.
I'd say I won't change my life **for a guess**.
think: Ten years feels like **forever**, so I'd give the Jobcentre a good few more years.
At **thirty-seven** I can still start Dad's joinery trade.
do: Go for the **team lead** job and keep saving.
Start **joinery evening classes** around year four or five.
feel: **Anxious** at a low level, sitting in the **background**.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever, and thirty-seven is still young enough to start in my dad's joinery trade.
fieldNote: With time, Sam slides back into **waiting**, fitting his resistance.
He'd delay **marriage** until his future is clear, a traditional view of providing.
His trigger to act is **staff not replaced** at his office.

steps.text: Apply for the Jobcentre team lead post
Put off joinery evening classes until year four or five
Pay off the house mortgage before 2036
Hold off on marriage until work feels settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no trade. What would help is proper apprenticeships for grown adults, paid, not just for school leavers. Let people like me learn a real skill with a wage while we do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people will still have a reason to get up in the morning. I see it every day with my claimants. Work gives you more than money, and a cheque from the government doesn't fix a man sitting at home all day.

headlineQuote: Work gives you more than money, and a cheque from the government doesn't fix a man sitting at home all day.
portrait: Sam is a **27-year-old** Jobcentre caseworker in a market town who has never used an AI tool.
He owns his house with a **small mortgage** and has over a year saved, partly inherited.
He's **traditional**: he values work, family trades and local hiring over handouts and technology.
In the AGI scenarios he falls back on his **dad's joinery** trade, but tends to **wait** first.
He stays calm only in AI Plateau and is **alarmed** when AGI arrives within five years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which leaves him with **no time** and **no trade**.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships**, so people can learn a skill on a wage.
